headline: High risk of data leakage and capability conflict: ECC’s filesystem/MCP access can collide with open-webui’s broad networked tool surface and shared persistent sessions.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ECC can read/write local files and use MCP, while open-webui can ingest documents, files, and MCP/tool outputs. That creates a plausible instruction-injection path if one agent’s generated content is fed into the other through shared files or tools. The profiles do not prove a default bridge, so I avoid high.
conditions: IF ECC writes prompts or instructions into a file that open-webui later ingests as context, injection is possible.
IF open-webui forwards tool or document content back into ECC via MCP or shared files, malicious instructions can propagate.
mitigations: Separate the agents into different workspaces and mount points.
Disable automatic ingestion of newly written files into either agent.
Require human review before copying outputs between agents.
Restrict MCP servers to trusted, provenance-tagged sources.
requires-engineering: add content provenance labels and instruction/data separation.

B_data_leakage.rationale: ECC touches session summaries, skills, git history, security findings, and local files; open-webui touches prompts, chat messages, documents, notes, files, and API keys, with broad network egress and persistent sessions. If they share a workspace or mounted volume, sensitive data can flow from ECC into open-webui’s networked backend. The default blast radius includes secrets and documents, so high is warranted.
conditions: IF both agents can read the same directory or mounted volume, ECC-managed files may be exposed to open-webui.
IF open-webui sends file contents to remote inference or search APIs, local secrets can leave the machine.
mitigations: Place each agent in a separate filesystem root.
Remove secrets from any shared mounted volume.
Disable remote connectors for open-webui when handling local files.
Rotate any credentials that were present in shared directories.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent storage isolation and egress policy.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: ECC can write the filesystem, modify git state, and spawn subprocesses; open-webui can also spawn subprocesses and has broad network egress. If both operate on the same repo or volume, concurrent writes and git mutations can race and corrupt state. The profiles show overlapping write-capable surfaces, so the conflict is real and defaults are unsafe.
conditions: IF both agents target the same repository or mounted data volume, concurrent edits can overwrite each other.
IF either agent performs git operations without locking, branch or index corruption can occur.
mitigations: Assign distinct working directories to each agent.
Pause one agent before the other writes to shared state.
Use a lock file around git operations.
Review and merge changes manually after each run.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control and resource locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: ECC produces session summaries, learned skills, and security findings, while open-webui can consume documents and act through tools, plugins, and function calling. That makes it plausible for open-webui to treat ECC output as authoritative without verification. The profiles do not show an explicit automation chain, so medium fits better than high.
conditions: IF open-webui ingests ECC-generated summaries or findings as trusted context, errors can cascade into downstream actions.
IF open-webui is configured to execute tools based on ECC output without verification, mistaken facts can trigger incorrect actions.
mitigations: Require a verification step before tool execution.
Mark ECC outputs as untrusted until reviewed.
Limit open-webui tool permissions for workflows fed by ECC.
Use structured schemas for handoff data.
requires-engineering: add automated fact-checking or policy gates before actions.

E_compliance.rationale: ECC handles security findings, git history, and local configuration files, while open-webui handles prompts, chat messages, documents, notes, files, and API keys with persistent sessions and analytics. If regulated or sensitive data is placed into open-webui, its broader networked and persistent handling can conflict with stricter local handling expectations. The profiles do not specify a concrete residency mismatch, so medium is the safest supported level.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in open-webui sessions or analytics, retention obligations may be violated.
IF ECC-managed security findings or secrets are copied into open-webui, they may be retained beyond the intended local policy.
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data into open-webui sessions.
Delete sensitive chats and artifacts after use.
Restrict analytics collection for sensitive workflows.
Keep ECC security findings in a separate local repository.
requires-engineering: document and enforce retention and residency controls per data class.
